title: Eighty questions in eight minutes
objectives: Practise the 80-in-8 format and pace yourself through it.

screens.prose: Some firms set an arithmetic test of 80 questions in 8 minutes. The mix runs from $291 + 883$ to $\tfrac23 - \tfrac12$ and the next term of a sequence. Before any question, work out the pace.
screens.question: How many seconds does each question get?

hints.text: Turn 8 minutes into seconds first.
8 minutes is 480 seconds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share 480 seconds over 80 questions.

byKey.per-minute: 10 is the number of questions a minute, $80 \div 8$. Each one gets 60 s over 10: 6 s.
byKey.flipped: You divided 8 by 80, which gives minutes: 0.1 of a minute is 6 s.

explain.text: 8 minutes is 480 seconds, and $480 \div 80 = 6$. Zetamac at 50 is 2.4 s an answer, so this pace is slower. The questions are harder, though, and four options sit beside each one.

screens.prose: The line is the 8 minutes of the test. Drag the point along it. The caption says how many questions you should have answered by then, at 6 seconds each.

derive.caption: At {{fixed(t.x, 1)}} minutes, on pace, you have answered {{round(t.x * 10)}} questions.

screens.question: Drag to 4 minutes. How many questions should be done by then?

hints.text: Move the point to 4 and read the caption.
Ten questions fit in each minute.

feedback.correct: Ten a minute: 40 at 4 minutes, halfway in time and in count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption with the point at 4 minutes.

byKey.times-six: You multiplied 4 by 6. Four minutes is 240 s, and $240 \div 6 = 40$.
byKey.minutes: 4 is the time. The count at 4 minutes is ten a minute: 40.

explain.text: At 6 s a question, ten fit in a minute. So 4 minutes is 40 questions, exactly half the paper. If you are below that count at 4 minutes, you are behind pace.

screens.prose: A **checkpoint** is the question you should have reached by a given minute. Write three before you start, and one glance at the clock tells you whether you are on pace.
screens.question: Drag Q20, Q40 and Q60 to the minute when each should be done.

hints.text: Twenty questions at 6 s each take how long?
20 questions take 120 s, which is 2 minutes.
Q20 at 2, Q40 at 4, Q60 at 6.

feedback.correct: Q20 at 2, Q40 at 4, Q60 at 6: twenty questions every two minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each block of 20 questions takes 2 minutes.

byKey.q20: Q20 at 6 s each is 120 s: 2 minutes.

explain.text: Every 20 questions is two minutes, so the checkpoints are 2, 4 and 6. Ten seconds behind at a checkpoint is under two questions. Steady up rather than race.

screens.prose: Some tests let you skip and come back. A question that takes 20 s costs three others at 6 s. You have 60 s left and ten questions, with the seconds each would take you.
screens.question: Tap the questions to skip, so that you answer as many as possible in 60 s.

hints.text: Which questions cost the most?
Q71 and Q72 take 22 s and 25 s.
Skip those two: the other eight take 58 s.

feedback.correct: Skip Q71 and Q72: the other eight take 58 s and all fit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the cheapest questions until the 60 s runs out.

byKey.slow-all: You skipped the two 14 s questions too. The eight cheapest take 58 s, inside 60, so keep them.
byKey.r0: Q71 takes 22 s, nearly four quick ones. Skip it.
byKey.r1: Q72 takes 25 s, the slowest. Skip it first.
byKey.r3: Q74 takes 14 s, but it still fits: the eight cheapest total 58 s.
byKey.r6: Q77 takes 14 s, but it still fits: the eight cheapest total 58 s.
byKey.r2: Q73 takes 4 s. Skipping a quick one wastes the easiest mark.
byKey.r4: Q75 takes 3 s, the cheapest. Keep it.
byKey.r5: Q76 takes 5 s. Keep the quick ones.
byKey.r7: Q78 takes 8 s, which fits easily.
byKey.r9: Q80 takes 6 s, exactly on pace. Keep it.

explain.text: Sorted, the costs run 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8, 14, 14, 22, 25. The first eight sum to 58 s; adding 22 would pass 60. Cheapest first always fits the most when every question scores the same.

screens.title: A block of twenty
screens.prose: Twenty questions in the test’s mix, four options each. Target: 2 minutes, 6 s a question. Nothing in this lesson is timed by the app, so start your own watch. When the block ends, take one breath, then note your time on paper.
screens.question: Type the letter of each answer.

hints.text: Estimate first, then let the last digit choose between close options.
$41 \times 24$ must end in 4, which rules out two options.
Q1 to Q5: B, D, D, B, D. Q6 to Q10: B, B, A, B, A. Q11 to Q15: D, B, D, C, A. Q16 to Q20: D, B, C, D, A.

feedback.correct: All twenty right. Compare your time with the 2-minute target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows, and note which kind each one was.

byKey.r0c2: Q1: Left to right: 842 + 400 = 1,242, then + 44 = 1,286. That is B.
byKey.r1c2: Q2: Times 2 each time: 24 × 2 = 48. That is D.
byKey.r2c2: Q3: Missing multiplication: 16 × 19 = 304, so 19. That is D.
byKey.r3c2: Q4: Round up: 972 − 220 = 752, then add back 1: 753. That is B.
byKey.r4c2: Q5: 52 × 3 = 156; 2 decimal places in all: 1.56. That is D.
byKey.r6c2: Q7: 10% is 32, times 3: 96. That is B.
byKey.r7c2: Q8: Double and take 4: 2 × 52 − 4 = 100. That is A.
byKey.r8c2: Q9: Left to right: 205 + 500 = 705, then + 41 = 746. That is B.
byKey.r10c2: Q11: 10% is 16, so 5% is half: 8. That is D.
byKey.r12c2: Q13: Round up: 592 − 590 = 2, then add back 3: 5. That is D.
byKey.r13c2: Q14: 73 × 8 = 584; 1 decimal place in all: 58.4. That is C.
byKey.r17c2: Q18: Missing multiplication: 18 × 93 = 1,674, so 93. That is C.
byKey.r18c2: Q19: Move both points 1 place: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. That is D.

explain.text: Each row took one move, such as left to right, a split, a moved point, a denominator or a difference. The last digit alone settles many options. The kind that took longest is your next drill.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: Candidates report this test as four options, +1 right and −1 wrong, forward only, with no skipping. The reported pass line is about 50 to 60 net. Rules vary by test and change each cycle. With no skip, a slow question becomes a fast guess.
screens.question: Fill in the average mark of a guess after removing 0, 1 or 2 options.

hints.text: A guess among 4 is right 1 time in 4.
Among 4: $\tfrac14 \times 1 + \tfrac34 \times (-1)$.

feedback.correct: $-0.5$, $-\tfrac13$, then $0$: each option removed makes the guess cheaper.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh +1 and −1 by the chance of each.

explain.text: A blind guess costs half a mark on average, and removing two options makes it free. So cut options fast, pick one and move on. Level 4 works out when a guess beats a blank.

screens.prose: Sam answers Q1 and Q2 in 6 s each, then spends 30 s on Q3 and gets it right. Sam plans to make the time up later.
screens.question: Sam then keeps exactly 6 s a question. How many questions does Sam reach in 480 s?

widget.label: Questions reached
widget.accept: 76: 438 s left after Q3 fits 73 more.

hints.text: Add up the time used by the end of Q3.
$6 + 6 + 30 = 42$ s, which leaves 438 s.

feedback.correct: Q3 cost 24 s over its share: four questions, so Sam reaches Q76.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the seconds left after Q3, at 6 s each.

byKey.catch-up: You assumed the 30 s comes back later. At a steady 6 s it never does: the last four questions go unreached.
byKey.five-off: You took off five questions for 30 s. Q3 itself was answered, so only 24 s were extra: four questions.

explain.text: Q3 used 24 s more than its share, so four questions at the end are never seen. Rushing the last 30 to catch up only raises the errors. That is the first-minute rule: settle the pace early and let a hard question go.

screens.prose: You shared the time out evenly. For $N$ questions in $T$ seconds, question $k$ is due at $$t_k = \frac{T}{N}\,k.$$ The first minute sets that pace. A question that costs far more than $\tfrac{T}{N}$ is skipped, or cut down and guessed.
screens.question: For 80 questions in 480 s, when is question 60 due, in seconds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the pace, 6 s, by 60.

byKey.minutes: 6 is the time in minutes. In seconds it is 360.
byKey.ten: 600 uses 10 s a question. The pace is $480 \div 80 = 6$ s.

explain.text: The pace is $\tfrac{480}{80} = 6$ s, so $t_{60} = 360$ s. That is 6 minutes, the third checkpoint. The same rule works for any test once you know $N$ and $T$.

screens.prose: Derive the checkpoints for 80 questions in 8 minutes. Put the lines in order, and leave out the one that confuses minutes with seconds.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: 8 minutes is 480 s, since a minute is 60 s
Each question gets $480 \div 80 = 6$ s, as every question scores the same
After $k$ questions on pace, $6k$ seconds have passed
So Q20 is due at 120 s, Q40 at 240 s and Q60 at 360 s
That is ten a minute: write 20, 40 and 60 against minutes 2, 4 and 6
Each question gets $8 \div 80 = 0.1$, so 10 s each
lines.why: $8 \div 80 = 0.1$ is in minutes: 0.1 of a minute is 6 s, not 10 s.

hints.text: Start by putting the time in seconds.
Then share it out, then multiply by $k$.
Seconds, share, multiply, the three times, then minutes.

feedback.correct: Seconds, the share, the rule, the three times, then the minutes to write down.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the time in seconds.

byKey.d1: $8 \div 80 = 0.1$ is in minutes: 0.1 of a minute is 6 s, not 10 s.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the 10-second one belongs.
byKey.s2: Share the time out once it is in seconds.
byKey.s3: The rule for question $k$ comes after the pace.
byKey.s4: Apply the rule to 20, 40 and 60 after stating it.
byKey.s5: The minutes to write down come last.

explain.text: Seconds first, then the share, then $t_k = 6k$. Q20, Q40 and Q60 fall at 120, 240 and 360 s. In minutes that is 2, 4 and 6.

screens.title: Skips and checkpoints in code
screens.prose: `best_skips(costs, budget)` returns the most questions you can answer in `budget` seconds, given the seconds each costs. `checkpoint_times(n, seconds, every)` returns when questions `every`, `2 * every`, ... are due, with the last question added if the steps miss it.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests: seven skip budgets (exact counts) and five checkpoint lists (`math.isclose` on each time).

hints.text: Sort the costs and keep adding until the next one would pass the budget.
Question $k$ is due at `seconds * k / n`.
Use `range(every, n + 1, every)`, then append `n` if it is missing.

feedback.correct: Both functions match the lesson: cheapest first, and $t_k = \tfrac{T}{N}k$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort before counting, and multiply the pace by each checkpoint.

explain.text: Sorting first makes the greedy count exact: no other choice fits more questions. `checkpoint_times(60, 540, 25)` adds question 60 because 25 and 50 miss the end. That last time is always the whole test.

screens.prose: Your real online test: 60 questions in 9 minutes, pen and paper allowed. Plan the room first: quiet, a charged laptop, a tested link, a phone out of reach. Then write the checkpoints at the top of your paper.
screens.question: Fill in the pace and the three checkpoints, in seconds.

hints.text: 9 minutes is 540 s.
$540 \div 60 = 9$ s a question.

feedback.correct: 9 s a question: Q15 at 135 s, Q30 at 270 s, Q45 at 405 s.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the pace, then multiply by 15, 30 and 45.

explain.text: The pace is $540 \div 60 = 9$ s, so the checkpoints are 2:15, 4:30 and 6:45. Write them in minutes and seconds, as the test clock shows them. Read the test’s own rules on skipping and marking before you start.

ideas: 80 in 8 is 6 s a question, ten a minute. Q20, Q40 and Q60 are due at 2, 4 and 6 minutes.
Where skipping is allowed, skip any question far over 6 s and come back; cheapest first fits the most.
Where it is not, cut options and guess: a blind guess is worth −0.5, and 0 after removing two.
summary.trap: Spending 30 s on question 3 costs four questions at the end, and the rush raises errors.

quiz.prose: A test that allows skipping. You reach the last question with 40 s left and three questions skipped.
quiz.question: What do you do with the 40 s?

options.text: Go back to the three skipped questions
Recheck the easy answers from the first block
options.why: You spent the spare time on answers that are most likely right already. A skip is a sure blank until you try it.

options.text: Stop: the score is already set
options.why: Unused time scores nothing. Spend it on the skips.

feedback.correct: Return to the skips: each is a blank until you try it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where a mark can still be gained.

byKey.recheck: You spent the spare time on answers that are most likely right already. A skip is a sure blank until you try it.
byKey.wait: Unused time scores nothing. Spend it on the skips.

explain.text: Finishing early is the time skip and return was saving. The skipped questions are the only blanks left. Rechecking easy ones rarely changes a mark.

quiz.prose: 80 questions in 8 minutes. At the 5-minute mark you are reading question 44.
quiz.question: How many questions behind pace are you?

feedback.correct: Pace at 5 minutes is Q50, so you are 6 behind.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the on-pace question at 5 minutes first.

byKey.sign: That says ahead. Pace is Q50 and you are at Q44: 6 behind.
byKey.seconds: 36 is the gap in seconds. In questions it is $36 \div 6 = 6$.

explain.text: Ten a minute puts pace at Q50 at 5 minutes. You are at Q44, six behind, which is 36 s. Close it by guessing faster, not by rushing every question.

quiz.prose: Four options, +1 for right and −1 for wrong.
quiz.question: What is a blind guess worth on average?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh +1 by the chance of right and −1 by the chance of wrong.

byKey.chance: 0.25 is the chance of being right. The 3 in 4 wrong answers each cost a mark.
byKey.cancel: +1 and −1 cancel only when right and wrong are equally likely, after removing two options.

explain.text: Right 1 time in 4 earns $\tfrac14$; wrong 3 times in 4 costs $\tfrac34$. On average a blind guess loses half a mark.

quiz.prose: A test that allows skipping. 60 s are left, and the questions would take you 4, 5, 6, 18, 7 and 25 s.
quiz.question: What is the most you can answer?

feedback.correct: Skip the 25 s one: the other five take 40 s.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the cheapest until the next would pass 60 s.

byKey.drop-18: You skipped the 18 s one too. With it the five take 40 s, still inside 60.
byKey.all: All six take 65 s, over the 60 s left.

explain.text: Sorted: 4, 5, 6, 7, 18, 25. The first five take 40 s and the 25 s one would make 65. So five, with 20 s to spare.
